texts.preamble: Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Author: S.C.Sharma Bench: S.C.Sharma Writ Petition No.19974/2019 1 High Court Of Madhya Pradesh: Bench At Indore Writ Petition No.19974/2019 Balmukund Garg v/s The State of Madhya Pradesh & Others Indore, dated 02.12.2019
texts.facts: The petitioner before this Court has filed this present petition being aggrieved by the order dated 24.08.2019 passed by the District Magistrate, Barwani under the provisions of National Security Act, 1980. 02. The petitioner's contention is that he is running a firm in the name and style of "M/s Balmukund Mohanlal" registered with the Food Department and on 05.08.2019, the officer of the Food Department conducted a raid at his premises and seized certain materials. The material was forwarded for analysis and F.I.R. was also registered in the matter. Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/ 1 05. A reply has been filed on behalf of respondents No.1 to 4 and it has been stated that a raid was conducted at the premises of the petitioner and samples of ghee, poha, vanaspati, palm oil and gud were seized from the premises of the petitioner and the materials were forwarded to the State Examination Laboratory. 06. The respondents have also stated that they have registered a F.I.R. for the offences under Sections 272, 273, 420 of the Indian Penal Code r/w Section 3 and 4 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.
texts.arguments: 03. It has been further contended that thereafter, an order of detention has been passed on 24.08.2019 under the provisions of National Security Act, 1980. It has been stated that only one case was registered against the father of the petitioner, Mohanlal i.e. Case No.33/2013 for the offence under Section 26(2)(ii) r/w section 52 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and a fine was imposed against his father on 31.07.2014. The petitioner's contention is that on the basis of solitary incident / registration of a case under the Food Safety and Standard Act, 2006, the petitioner could not have been detained under the National Security Act, 1980. 04. Reliance has been placed upon a judgment delivered in the case of Rinku @ Kuldeep Shukla v/s The State of Madhya Pradesh & Others reported in 2015 (3) MPLJ 157. The petitioner has stated that he is a trader. He is neither proprietor nor partner of the firm M/s Balmukunt Mohanlal, and therefore, merely because some food articles were misbranded, he cannot be punished in the manner and method it has been done in the present case. The respondents have stated that keeping in view the misbranded and adulterated food articles, they have rightly passed an order under the National Security Act, 1980. 09. A Division Bench of this Court in the case of Sudeep Jain v/s The State of Madhya Pradesh & Others (W.P. No.21768/2019) Paragraph - 4 to 21 of the aforesaid judgment reads as under :- "4. In 1951, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court while examining the ambit and scope of section 12 of the "Preventive Detention Act, 1950", held that the Act does not require the period of detention to be mentioned1. In Suna Ullah Butt's case, a three judge bench of the Supreme Court while examining the scope of section 12 and 13 of the "Jammu and Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 1964" held "The second contention of Mr Om Prakash relates to the fact that the period for which the petitioner was to be detained has not been mentioned in the order of the State Government, dated March 3, 1972, confirming the detention order. It is urged that the failure of the State Government to specify the period of detention introduces an infirmity in the detention of the petitioner. This contention, in our opinion, is without any force........ The concluding words of subsection (1) of Section 12, according to which the Government may continue the detention of the person concerned for such period as it thinks fit, pertain to and embody the Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/ 2 consequence of the confirmation of the detention order"2. 5. However, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court in Gurbux Anandram Bhiryani's case held otherwise. In a brief order, the Supreme Court while examining an in pari materia provision in the "Maharashtra Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Slumlords, Bootleggers and Drug Offenders Act, 1981" held "The order is bad on another ground, namely, the period of detention has not been indicated by the detaining authority. The scheme of this Act differs from the provisions contained in similar Acts by not prescribing a period of detention but as Section 3 of the Act indicates, there is an initial period of detention which can extend up to three months and that can be extended for periods of three months at a time. It was open to the detaining authority to detain the detenu even for a period of lesser duration than three months. That necessitated the period of detention to be specified and unless that was indicated in the order, the order would also be vitiated"3. 6. This order passed by the two-judge bench of the Supreme Court was expressly overruled by a three- judge bench of the Supreme Court in T.Devaki's case where the Supreme Court once again reiterated the position in Ujagar Singh and Suna Ullah Butt's case. The Court held "The Act nowhere requires the detaining authority to specify the period for which the detenu is required to be detained. The expression "the State Government are satisfied that it is necessary so to do, they may, by order in writing direct that during such period as may be specified in the order" occurring in sub- section (2) of Section 3 relates to the period for which the order of delegation issued by the State Government is to remain in force and it has no relevance to the period of detention"4. 7. As recently as 2018, the view expressed in T. Devaki's case was once again considered and approved of by another three-judge bench of the Supreme Court where it held "In T. Devaki v. State of T.N. [T. Devaki v. State of T.N., (1990) 2 SCC 456 : 1990 SCC (Cri) 348] , a Bench of this Court has held that since the legislation does not require the detaining authority to specify the period for which a detenu is required to be detained, the order of detention is not rendered invalid or illegal in the absence of such specification..... In the circumstances, the High Court was not justified in quashing the order of detention on the basis that no period of detention was provided in the order. The High Court has proceeded on the basis of the decision of this Court in Bhiryani [Commr. of Police v. Gurbux Anandram Bhiryani, 1988 Supp SCC 568 : 1988 SCC (Cri) 914] which is no longer good law in view of the subsequent decision of a larger Bench in Devaki [T. Devaki v. State of T.N., (1990) 2 SCC 456 : 1990 SCC (Cri) 348]...."5. Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/ 3 8. Thus, on the basis of the judgements of the Supreme Court mentioned hereinabove, this Court holds that an order of detention under the NSA is not vitiated, merely because it does not specify the period of detention, as there is no provision in the NSA mandating such a requirement. In this regard this Court feels that the obiter dicta in Gurbux Anandram Bhiriyani's case is relevant. 9. The Ld. Counsel for the Petitioner has submitted that the grounds of detention served upon him inform him that he has a right to represent to the State Government and that he has a right to audience before the Advisory Board to present his case. This right to represent to the detaining authority itself was examined by the Supreme Court in Santosh Shankar Acharya's case where the Court examined the right of a detenu to make a representation to the detaining authority and the effect of non-communication to the detenu of the said right, under the "Maharashtra Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Slumlords, Bootleggers, Drug-Offenders and Dangerous Persons Act, 1981". Thereafter, the Supreme Court examined the non-communication to the detenu, his right to represent to the detaining authority in the following words, "...This being the position, noncommunication of the fact to the detenu that he could make a representation to the detaining authority so long as the order of detention has not been approved by the State Government in a case where an order of detention is issued by an officer other than the State Government under sub-section (2) of section 3of the Maharashtra Act would constitute an infraction of a valuable right of the detenu under Article 22(5) of the Constitution..."6 13. Earlier, in the year 1995, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court also held as above in the case of Kamlesh Kumar Ishwardas Patel. The Court held that "Article 22(5) must therefore, be construed to mean that the person detained has a right to make a representation against the order of detention which can be made not only to the Advisory Board but also to the detaining authority, i.e., the authority that has made the order of detention or the order for the continuance of such detention, which is competent to give immediate relief by revoking the said order as well as to any other authority which is competent under law to revoke the order for detention and thereby give relief to the person detained. The right to make a representation carries within it a corresponding obligation on the authority making the order of detention to inform the person detained of his right to make a representation against the order of detention to the authorities who are required to consider such an application"7. The satisfaction of the District Magistrate for detaining the Petitioner under the NSA is reflected in paragraph 2 of the grounds which reads thus;" ! ! , Magistrate arrives at the finding that in the case against the Petitioner, the report of the analyst has Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/ 5 established that seized food material is of sub-standard quality. In the same paragraph, the District Magistrate arrives at the finding that "... 1 ! / In another place in the same paragraph, the District Magistrate opines " 78 " or that on account of the activity of the Petitioner, there is a health hazard posed to human life. 15. (b) the FSSA does not even provide for the punishment of imprisonment for the sale of "sub-standard" food and makes the act punishable only with fine as is provided under section 51 of the FSSA which reads "Any person who whether by himself or by any other person on his behalf manufactures for sale or stores or sells Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/ 6 or distributes or imports any article of food for human consumption which is sub-standard, shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to five lakh rupees" 18. In this regard, it would be relevant to refer to the opinion of the Supreme Court in a case of preventive detention based upon a single case under the provisions of the IPC, where the Supreme Court held that ".....An individual incident under the Penal Code, however heinous, is insufficient to make out a case for issuance of an order of preventive detention"8. 19. In this regard, the opinion of the Supreme Court is extremely relevant where it held "Preventive detention is, by nature, repugnant to democratic ideas and an anathema to the rule of law. It follows, therefore, that if the ordinary law of the land (the Penal Code and other penal statutes) can deal with a situation, recourse to a preventive detention law will be illegal"9. 20. Regulatory Statutes are laws that are made by the legislature to regulate the conduct of certain human activities. Where the State resorts to proceedings under the NSA against individuals, whose actions are violations under regulatory statutes, and whose liberty is infringed by the State and its functionaries by a perverse Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/ 7 and contorted interpretation of the phrase "public order", the same shall attract severe indictment of the State and the officers responsible for such malicious exercise of executive discretion.
